title: Target employee tells woman at self-checkout section ‘You can’t leave.’ It turns out they actually saved her life
content:
Women’s safety is a rising concern in modern society. Each day we switch on the news to hear about another woman getting harassed or assaulted in public places. Even shopping centers and convenience stores covered with security cameras do not help much in dangerous situations. A woman named Nina Sotom (@ninasotom on TikTok) was out at her local Target to do some shopping, when she experienced something truly terrifying. In her TikTok video, Sotom mentioned that while she was about to make her exit after the shopping spree and reached the store’s self-checkout counter, Target’s security personnel stopped her from leaving.
What the security team actually stopped her for
Initially, Sotom was confused, but she gradually came to know the real reason behind the security personnel’s action. While Sotom was busy browsing, the security person was actually keeping an eye on her. After clearing her purchase and collecting her payment, the Target staff informed Sotom that she still wasn’t allowed to leave. Sotom thought she was possibly being detained because they suspected her of shoplifting. “I remember grabbing my receipt and holding it flat out because I know that little camera up there can read the smallest print,” Sotom recalled.
The Target staff then spoke to another lady while Sotom waited. In time, the other woman, who turned out to be another security worker, shared a shocking revelation with Sotom: a suspicious fellow was following her around the store and sneakily taking her picture. “I’m so sorry I didn’t catch it earlier, I would have thrown him out,” the security worker apologized, according to Sotom. The security worker then assured Sotom that the troublesome man was out of the shop at that point and no longer posed her any harm. To be extra safe, the security worker then escorted Sotom to her car.
Her reaction says it all
Sotom was thankful for everything the Target security team did to keep her safe from what could have been an extremely dangerous situation. “Even if that man was just being creepy and sending those pictures to a random person, it makes me as a woman feel so secure and so safe to know that other people are watching out for me and it’s not just me watching out for me,” she reflected in her video. In a separate comment under the video, Sotom elaborated that her mom ended up calling the police and they contacted the Target store. They were taking the cautionary steps just to be on the safe side. The comment section applauded the alert security for their vigilance and professionalism.
The comments were full of similar stories
One commenter recalled, “This happened to me. I am 9 months pregnant and I was shopping alone with my 3 boys. A man was following us around and taking pictures of my kids. The worker was telling me I couldn’t leave. I promised that my kids or I did not steal and then I was told that a man was following me.”
Another applauded Target security, saying, “They’re the best! When I got my husband the new Xbox. It was wild that they had two guys escort me to my car because people would wait outside to snatch it.”
This viewer commented, “I didn’t even imagine this is where your story would go. This is so scary glad you’re safe.”
Another added, “Wow that’s awesome. I was not expecting that outcome! So glad to hear she was just trying to take care of you!”
Next time you’re out shopping, rest assured there are security teams looking out for your safety, but don’t let it stop there. Keep an eye out for your fellow shoppers, too. If everyone is looking out for one another, we’ll all be a lot safer in this world.

title: Manal bounces back after failing to make it to u-19 WC team
content:
Manal Chauhan started playing cricket for a simple reason — he wanted to bunk school.
He would tell his parents he was going to school and head off to play cricket instead. “At that time, I was not that interested in the sport, but I kept playing,” Manal told The Hindu ahead of Monday’s second youth ODI between India under-19 and the Australian colts here.
“Gradually, I realised that there were age-group divisions and that you move forward through them and then play for the State. I became very interested in it, so I started giving it my full time.”
The boy from Morena has since led Madhya Pradesh to its maiden Cooch Behar Trophy title and made his India u-19 debut on the Sri Lanka tour, scoring 150 and an unbeaten 51 in the second youth Test.
But it wasn’t a smooth ride. After a decent Vinoo Mankad Trophy campaign, the all-rounder missed out on the u-19 World Cup. “I was very demotivated because I wanted to play the World Cup. At that time, I did not know that there would be further bilateral series like this,” he said.
His parents and coaches told him there would be more opportunities. “I thought that, at least, I would win the red-ball tournament for MP. I did not know that I would come this far from there.”
Madhya Pradesh did win the Cooch Behar Trophy. Then came the India call-up.
“The biggest learning has been that things will keep going up and down in life, but you have to stick to your work ethic,” he said.
Chandrakant Pandit has helped him work on the mental side of the game, while India u-19 coach Yere Goud taught him to forget mistakes and move on.
Manal is doing just that, taking it one step at a time.

title: Jesús María: mujer de 63 años recibió cita para completar sus exámenes preoperatorios en el Hospital Rebagliati
content:
La mujer, de 63 años, sufre de cataratas avanzadas y miopía.
Fabiola Nizama Canepa se comunicó con el Rotafono de RPP para informar que obtuvo sus citas para realizarse sus exámenes preoperatorios por las cataratas avanzadas y miopía, enfermedades que padece y son tratadas en el Hospital Nacional Edgardo Rebagliati Martins, de EsSalud, en el distrito limeño de Jesús María.
Fabiola cuenta que, después de que su caso fue difundido en el Rotafono de RPP, las autoridades de salud se comunicaron con ella para darle seguimiento y pudo obtener sus citas para realizar su examen de ecobiometría este 24 de setiembre; la microscopia especular este 25 de septiembre y la cita en neumología este 28 del mismo mes.
"Me han llamado citas de EsSalud y me han dado cita el día 24, 25 y 28. Espero pronto se haga realidad mi operación y pido a EsSalud que acelere la cita para los adultos mayores”, afirmó Fabiola Nizama.
La paciente agradeció que EsSalud haya escuchado su pedido de ayuda y demandó un trato digno para los adultos mayores.
“Señores de RPP, agradezco mucho a Rotafono por haber hecho público mi caso sobre la falta de citas preoperatorias, que desde el año pasado venía esperando. Pido a EsSalud que acelere la atención de los adultos mayores, que tengamos un trato digno", expresó.
La mujer de 63 años sufre de cataratas avanzadas y miopía. Según contó, inicialmente se trataba en el Hospital Carlos Alcántara, pero los especialistas la derivaron al Hospital Rebagliati debido a la complejidad de su caso.
Fabiola Nizama Canepa se había comunicado con el Rotafono de RPP para reportar que espera desde el año pasado que se realicen la totalidad de sus exámenes prequirúrgicos para que programen su operación a la vista en el Hospital Rebagliati.

title: Infomaniak, l’acteur suisse qui milite pour l’autonomie numérique européenne
content:
Le nouveau quartier se nomme La Bistoquette, en lisière de l’agglomération genevoise, adossé à la frontière française. Sous forme de coopérative d’habitation participative, ce lotissement de plusieurs centaines de logements, posé dans un cadre de verdure foisonnante, dispose de tous les attributs du repaire bobo : vélos-cargos à foison, zéro déchets et épicerie bio où l’on peut commander un matcha au lait d’avoine dans un gobelet compostable. Mais c’est en sous-sol d’un immeuble que le spectacle prend toute son ampleur, sans dénaturer l’esprit des lieux.
Là, dans un long corridor bétonné, derrière des portes sécurisées par un double contrôle (empreinte digitale et biométrie), une armada de serveurs informatiques clignotent et bourdonnent, dans la chaleur aussi sèche qu’étouffante provoquée par leur activité. Au cœur des machines, la température des microprocesseurs peut monter jusqu’à 82 degrés. Pourtant, le tout nouveau centre de données D4 d’Infomaniak, le leader suisse des services numériques, n’utilise aucune climatisation. L’air extérieur, savamment filtré et brassé, suffit à refroidir les machines. Mieux, la chaleur dégagée n’est pas perdue, mais injectée dans le réseau de chaleur du Grand Genève.

title: Bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy cứu hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ở Phú Quốc
content:
Bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy cứu hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ở Phú Quốc
Hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim được bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy phối hợp Bệnh viện Mặt trời Phú Quốc (An Giang) can thiệp tái thông mạch vành kịp thời.
Ngày 20/9, BS.CK2 Lý Ích Trung, Trưởng khoa Tim mạch can thiệp Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, cho biết đây là hai ca can thiệp đầu tiên sau khi hai bệnh viện ký hợp tác chuyên môn hồi tháng 7. Bệnh nhân đầu tiên, 65 tuổi, nhập viện với triệu chứng khó thở, tức ngực, choáng váng, vã mồ hôi, tiền sử hút thuốc lá nhiều. Điện tâm đồ cho thấy bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ST chênh lên thành dưới.
Bác sĩ Nguyễn Tuấn Anh, Khoa Can thiệp tim mạch Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, vừa được điều động đến Phú Quốc tối hôm trước, phối hợp êkíp địa phương can thiệp cho bệnh nhân. Động mạch vành phải được tái thông thành công, dòng chảy phục hồi tốt, bệnh nhân giảm tức ngực và khó thở.
Ngay sau đó, bệnh viện tiếp nhận người đàn ông 58 tuổi, có tiền sử hút thuốc lá. Ông mệt và khó thở kéo dài, khám sức khỏe phát hiện điện tim bất thường nên được kiểm tra chuyên sâu. Kết quả cho thấy chức năng co bóp thất trái giảm, phân suất tống máu khoảng 45%, người bệnh được chẩn đoán nhồi máu cơ tim bán cấp thành trước, suy tim mức độ 2, rối loạn lipid máu và đái tháo đường. Bác sĩ can thiệp tái thông thành công đoạn động mạch bị tắc, dòng chảy phục hồi tốt.
Theo bác sĩ Trung, nhồi máu cơ tim ST chênh lên là thể có nguy cơ tử vong cao, cần tái thông động mạch vành càng sớm càng tốt. Nếu không được xử trí tại Phú Quốc, người bệnh phải chuyển vào đất liền để can thiệp, kéo dài thêm thời gian cấp cứu. Mỗi giờ chậm trễ can thiệp có thể làm tăng nguy cơ tử vong cho bệnh nhân khoảng 5-10%.
"Thời gian từ khi tiếp nhận đến khi can thiệp càng ngắn thì càng hạn chế vùng cơ tim bị tổn thương và giảm biến chứng", bác sĩ nói. Cả hai bệnh nhân được theo dõi sau can thiệp và vừa xuất viện trong tình trạng ổn định.
Theo BS.CK2 Phạm Thanh Việt, Giám đốc Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, chương trình hợp tác với Bệnh viện Mặt trời Phú Quốc nhằm kết nối chuyên môn, hỗ trợ xử trí các ca bệnh phức tạp ngay tại địa phương, đặc biệt là nhồi máu cơ tim cấp và đột quỵ não. Chợ Rẫy đã điều động bác sĩ chuyên khoa đến Phú Quốc, phối hợp với đội ngũ tại chỗ trong cấp cứu và điều trị, hướng đến giảm chuyển bệnh nhân vào đất liền.

title: Kazakhstan AI Training Expands Nationwide as Programs Scale Up
content:
Kazakhstan is expanding a free school for programming and artificial intelligence (AI) to 14 regions as part of a national drive to prepare people to use the technology. Government figures show that more than 100,000 university students have completed advanced AI courses, but evidence of what the training is producing in practice remains limited.
Tomorrow School offers adults a free 18-month course in programming and AI. It began operating outside Astana in 2026, and its network now covers 14 regions, with further growth planned across the country. Students need no previous programming experience and learn through practical projects and peer-to-peer instruction.
The school currently has 493 students, and according to government figures, 57 participants have already found jobs in the information technology sector. Few published statistics from Kazakhstan’s growing AI-training system report employment outcomes rather than enrollment or course completion.
TUMO Astana is a free center for teenagers aged 12 to 18, based on an educational model first developed in Armenia in 2011 and since expanded internationally. TUMO combines self-directed learning with workshops and practical projects in technology and design, including programming, robotics, and generative AI.
The center currently has 2,376 active students. By the end of 2026, it plans to increase enrollment to 5,000.
The largest enrollment is in AI-Sana, a national program aimed at giving university students AI skills and helping them develop their own technology projects. Students can take courses through Coursera, Huawei ICT Academy, the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute, and Astana Hub.
More than 100,000 students have completed advanced training under the program, receiving more than 703,000 certificates between them. Because participants can complete several courses, the certificate total is much higher than the number enrolled.
Of more than 22,000 proposed AI projects, 515 are now being tested or implemented, according to government figures. That total may be more revealing than the certificate count, although the announcement neither describes the work nor identifies where it is taking place.
In 2027, organizers plan to help 1,500 student teams develop their projects into technology startups.
Kazakhstan’s focus on retraining reflects changes in the labor market. The World Economic Forum estimates that 39% of workers’ existing skills will change or become outdated by 2030, while AI and big data are among the fastest-growing areas of demand.
The International Labour Organization cautions against equating the spread of AI with the disappearance of jobs, saying generative AI is more likely to transform jobs by automating some tasks than to replace workers entirely.
For more advanced training and research, Kazakhstan has established Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU). Since September 2026, it has offered two bachelor’s programs, one in AI and Machine Learning and the other in Physical AI, along with graduate programs combining AI with fields including finance, energy, medicine, industry, and public administration.
The university has 525 students: 388 undergraduates, 32 master’s students, and 105 participants from national companies in its AI+X Executive MBA program.

title: Woman loses 56 kg in 1.5 years, shifts focus to muscle gain and strength
content:
A middle-aged woman recently documented her fitness journey of losing 56 kgs in about 1.5 years. On a reel showing her transformation, Anureet Kaur commented on a user’s question about her weight loss and detailed, “It took me 1.5 years. I started in January 2024 and lost a total of 56 kg. Since then (2025), I have shifted my focus to muscle gain and strength.”
DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.
Consultant dietitian and fitness expert Garima Goyal called it a “powerful” story, noting that it is not just the number on the scale, but that she didn’t just get lighter—she got stronger. “In a world where most people still equate weight loss with eating less, skipping meals, or chasing crash diets, this story proves that the real goal should be fat loss with muscle preservation and strength gain,” said Goyal.
It means showing up on days when motivation is low, choosing structured meals over impulsive eating, training regularly, managing cravings, improving sleep, and staying patient even when progress slows down. “But gaining muscle during the process shows that her approach was likely not based on starvation. It reflects a smarter strategy: adequate protein, progressive strength training, controlled calories, and recovery,” said Goyal.
Sharing that people often focus only on reducing weight quickly, Goyal said that if the diet is too restrictive, the body loses not only fat but also muscle. “That may make the weighing scale drop, but it can also lead to weakness, loose skin, fatigue, poor metabolism, cravings, and weight regain. When muscle is preserved or gained during weight loss, the body becomes more toned, stronger, and metabolically healthier,” said Goyal.
Strength training plays a major role in this kind of transformation. “Cardio may help burn calories and improve stamina, but strength training gives the body shape. It helps build muscle, improves posture, supports bone health, increases functional strength, and improves insulin sensitivity. For someone losing a large amount of weight, resistance training is especially important because it helps the body look firm and athletic rather than simply smaller,” said Goyal.
Protein also becomes non-negotiable. “During fat loss, adequate protein helps repair muscles, improves satiety, reduces unnecessary hunger, and supports recovery after workouts. A well-balanced plate should include protein, fibre-rich carbohydrates, healthy fats, and enough micronutrients so that the body continues to function well while losing weight. Weight loss should never come at the cost of hair fall, weakness, menstrual disturbance, mood swings, or poor immunity,” Goyal told indianexpress.com.
A 56 kg transformation also highlights the importance of mindset. “No one loses that much weight through one perfect week. It happens through hundreds of repeated decisions — walking when it feels easier to sit, eating balanced meals when cravings hit, lifting weights when the body feels tired, and restarting after setbacks instead of giving up. The journey is not linear. There are plateaus, slow weeks, water-weight fluctuations, emotional eating phases, and moments of doubt. What matters is returning to the routine again and again,” reflected Goyal.
View this post on Instagram
However, such transformations should not be copied blindly. “Every person has a different starting weight, medical history, hormonal profile, lifestyle, stress level, and metabolism. Losing 56 kg in one year is a major achievement, but the safest pace and method will vary from person to person. For some, slower weight loss may be healthier and more sustainable. The focus should always be on preserving health while improving body composition,” cautioned Goyal.
The biggest takeaway from this transformation is that successful weight loss is not about punishment. It is not about starving, cutting out every favourite food, or doing endless cardio. It is about structure. It is about eating enough of the right foods, training consistently, sleeping properly, staying hydrated, and building habits that can continue even after the goal is reached.

title: ‘Our focus is weakening the Russian army’: For four years, Grigory Sverdlin’s aid group has helped Russians evade the draft and desert
content: In September 2022, immediately after Putin announced “partial” mobilization, Grigory Sverdlin, the former director of Nochlezhka, a foundation that helps the homeless, launched Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”). For four years now, the project has been helping Russians avoid taking part in the war — evading mobilization or deserting. To date, the organization has helped more than 82,000 people. In his book “Punkt Obogreva” (“Warming Station”), which was published by Meduza’s publishing house, Sverdlin describes the launch of Idite Lesom in detail. We are publishing an excerpt from the book about the project’s creation and its earliest days, translated into English.

title: Support from the U.S. Provides Food and Wheelchairs to Elderly in Camagüey
content:
A shipment containing essential supplies like food and wheelchairs has been dispatched from the United States to assist the elderly residents of the Monseñor Adolfo Home in Camagüey. This initiative has been made possible through generous donations from a Florida-based company, devoted Catholic followers, and members of the Camagüeyan exile community.
Details about this humanitarian effort were shared on Facebook by a page associated with the Monseñor Adolfo Home. The post extended gratitude to all those who facilitated the delivery of the container.
The food supplies were significantly contributed by Juan and Rosa Guixens of Guixens Food Group, a U.S. company specializing in the import and distribution of ethnic food products.
Founded in Florida in 1993, Guixens Food Group is headquartered in Miami and is recognized as a family-owned business. Besides its main operations in Miami, the company also maintains commercial activities in other U.S. locations, including Tampa, Atlanta, and New Jersey.
“Our heartfelt thanks to everyone who helped send this container filled with food and wheelchairs for the elderly at our Monseñor Adolfo Home in Camagüey,” the Facebook post stated.
The message specifically acknowledged Juan and Rosa Guixens “for the invaluable pallets of food” and the Catholic faithful who contributed the wheelchairs.
The post also highlighted the involvement of the board and members of the Municipality of Camagüey in Exile, a Florida-registered organization connected to the Camagüeyan community residing in Miami. Their donation was crucial in making the shipment possible.
“May God return this generosity in health and blessings and fill you with joy for doing a good deed,” the message concluded.
This aid arrives at a particularly challenging time for many elderly Cubans, who are struggling with inadequate pensions, high food prices, and shortages of basic necessities.
Earlier this year, it was reported that several social dining facilities for the elderly continued to operate thanks to donations coordinated by Catholic organizations.
One such donation enabled the distribution of nearly 1,000 kilograms of chickpeas across seven dining facilities in Havana, Camagüey, and Matanzas.
Despite their efforts, churches and religious organizations have faced obstacles.
In early September, a pastor from the municipality of Minas reported that authorities prevented his congregation from distributing breakfasts to the elderly and sick in the streets, forcing beneficiaries to travel to the church to receive their meals.

Elderly Cubans are dealing with insufficient pensions, high food prices, and shortages of essential goods, making daily life increasingly difficult.

Guixens Food Group, founded in Miami, contributed a significant portion of the food supplies sent to Camagüey, showcasing their commitment to helping those in need.

title: Over 7.18 lakh students appear for West Bengal Board HS Semester-3 exam 2027
content:
Over 7.18 lakh students appeared in the Higher Secondary Semester-III examination, which began on Monday, the West Bengal Council of Higher Education (WBCHSE) said.
A total of 7,18,620 candidates sat for the first language paper, including 3,15,731 male and 4,02,889 female students, according to the council. The exam was held from 11 am to 12.30 pm.
The examinations are being held from September 21 to October 14, with the schedule partially revised following the announcement of by-elections in Nandigram and Rejinagar on October 6 and in view of holidays.
Read | Check West Bengal Board HS Semester-3 exam 2027 detailed timetable
The exams were conducted at 825 centres covering 2,105 venues, including 99 identified as sensitive, the council said.
No untoward incident was reported during the examination on Monday, it said.
For the first time, the Semester-III examination is using OMR sheets for evaluation. The council has tied up with India Post for collection and transportation of completed OMR answer sheets from examination centres to its regional offices.
WBCHSE president Mosiur Rahaman Sardar said two invigilators were deployed in every examination room, maintaining a ratio of one invigilator for every 20 students.
“Mobile phones, calculators and other electronic gadgets were prohibited inside the examination venues. If any candidate is found carrying a mobile phone or electronic gadget, the examination and enrolment of the candidate will be cancelled,” Sardar said.
He said metal-detector frisking was conducted at the main gates of examination centres and CCTV surveillance was maintained at the gates and venue supervisors’ rooms.
Question papers bore unique serial numbers and sealed packets were opened in front of students before the examination, as part of measures to prevent malpractice and question paper leaks.
The council president also urged students not to pay heed to rumours or misinformation during the examination process.
The ongoing Semester-III examination is part of the semester system introduced by the WBCHSE for Classes 11 and 12.

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ Odienné: 51 élèves de familles vulnérables bénéficient d’un appui de plus de 9 millions FCFA
content:
Odienné, 18 sept 2026 (AIP)- Cinquante et un élèves issus de familles en situation de vulnérabilité ont bénéficié, vendredi 18 septembre 2026 à Odienné, de kits scolaires et d’un appui financier de 9 185 700 francs CFA, dans le cadre de l’initiative « Secours sociaux » du ministère de l’Emploi, de la Protection sociale et de la Formation professionnelle.
Cette action vise à soutenir les familles confrontées à des difficultés financières susceptibles de compromettre la scolarité de leurs enfants.
La directrice régionale de la Protection sociale et de la Formation professionnelle, Alla Guy Raïssa Koné, a expliqué que l’appui financier couvre les arriérés de frais de scolarité de l’année scolaire 2025-2026 ainsi que les frais de scolarité de l’année 2026-2027.
Il est complété par la remise de kits scolaires destinés aux élèves bénéficiaires afin d’alléger davantage les charges des familles et de favoriser de meilleures conditions d’apprentissage.
« Cette prise en charge couvre à la fois les arriérés de frais de scolarité de l’année scolaire 2025-2026 et les frais de scolarité de l’année scolaire en cours, 2026-2027 », a précisé Mme Koné.
Le député suppléant d’Odienné, Yacouba Savané, a rassuré les populations du Kabadougou quant à l’attention portée par l’État à leurs préoccupations, notamment dans les domaines de l’éducation et de la protection sociale.
« Cette action en faveur des élèves en est une illustration parfaite », a-t-il déclaré, au nom du ministre de l’Emploi, de la Protection sociale et de la Formation professionnelle, Adama Kamara.
Le préfet de la région du Kabadougou, René Famy Kouamé, a salué cette initiative en faveur des familles vulnérables et exhorté les bénéficiaires à faire bon usage de l’appui reçu.
L’initiative « Secours sociaux » s’inscrit dans les actions du gouvernement visant à renforcer la protection sociale et à favoriser l’accès et le maintien à l’école des enfants issus de familles confrontées à des difficultés sociales et économiques.

title: Free spectacles, hearing aids programme launched for university students
content:
The President’s Fund has launched a programme to provide free spectacles and hearing aids to university students, with the first programme held at Rajarata University on Saturday (19).
The initiative included free eye examinations and prescription lenses, with support from the private sector.
Spectacle frames donated to the President’s Fund are also planned to be distributed free of charge to schoolchildren, university students, technical college students and low-income citizens.
Senior Additional Secretary to the President and Secretary to the President’s Fund Roshan Gamage said the programme is expected to be extended to all universities in the future.
He also said the President’s Fund had strengthened by 50% over the past two years due to improved management and that its benefits were reaching eligible recipients across the country. (Newswire)

وذكرت قناة” الأقصى” الفلسطينية أن ذلك يأتي وسط واقع تعليمي استثنائي، لا تزال فيه غالبية المدارس خارج الخدمة، ويضطر فيه الطلبة إلى التعلم داخل خيام ومساحات مؤقتة، أو عبر التعليم عن بُعد.
وأشارت إلى أن العودة تأتي في ظل تضرر أو تدمير غالبية المباني التعليمية، فيما تحولت مدارس أخرى إلى مراكز لإيواء النازحين، ما جعل استئناف الدراسة مختلفًا عن الأعوام السابقة، بعدما لم تعد العملية التعليمية مرتبطة بالضرورة بالفصول والمقاعد المدرسية التقليدية.
وتستهدف خطة وزارة التربية والتعليم في غزة نحو 350 ألف طالب وطالبة هذا العام، مقارنة بنحو 270 ألفًا العام الماضي، فيما تعتمد وكالة غوث وتشغيل اللاجئين الفلسطينيين (أونروا) نموذجًا يجمع بين التعليم الحضوري والتعليم عن بُعد، يستهدف مئات الآلاف من الطلبة.
وقال مدير عام العلاقات العامة والإعلام في وزارة التربية والتعليم بغزة، أحمد عايش النجار، إن الوزارة وضعت خطة للتعليم المرن، انطلاقًا من أن حق الأطفال في التعليم لا يمكن أن ينتظر إعادة إعمار المدارس.
وأوضح النجار، في تصريح صحافي، أن الخطة تشمل المدارس الصالحة للاستخدام، ومراكز التعليم المؤقتة، ونقاط التعليم المقامة داخل الخيام، إلى جانب المنصات والتقنيات الرقمية، حيثما تتوفر الإمكانات، مؤكدًا أن استئناف الدراسة لا يعني بالضرورة عودة جميع الطلبة إلى مبانٍ مدرسية تقليدية.
من جانبه، أشار المتحدث باسم وكالة “أونروا”، عدنان أبو حسنة، إلى افتتاح 86 مساحة تعلم مع بداية العام الدراسي، على أن يتوسع التعليم الحضوري تدريجيًا، وفق توافر شروط السلامة والجاهزية والمساحة والمعلمين والخدمات الأساسية.
(د ب أ)

title: Belarus frees 25 political prisoners in return for US sanctions relief
content:
Belarus frees 25 political prisoners in return for US sanctions relief
The Trump administration said more releases would be secured soon amid improved US-Belarus relations.
Belarus on Wednesday freed 25 political prisoners as the United States lifted sanctions on two of the reclusive country’s companies, US envoy John Coale announced after his latest visit to Minsk.
The release on Wednesday marked the culmination of a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Those freed include human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where the freed prisoners were taken, Coale said he expected to return in about a month when he hopes to see “hundreds” freed.
The US envoy praised US President Donald Trump on social media, saying his “commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results” and that the administration would continue to “improve US-Belarus relations”.
Coale had been tasked by Trump with securing the release of hundreds of people. In March, the government of Belarus released 250 prisoners following a pardon.
Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The releases came a day after Coale promised Lukashenko that US banks would return tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
The US envoy earlier said that the US would lift sanctions on Lakokraska, a paint and industrial coating manufacturer, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial enterprise that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors.
Christian Wigand, the European Union’s lead spokesperson for foreign affairs and security policy, said the 25 prisoners were released as a result of US efforts.
“We welcome this step,” he wrote on X. “800+ individuals remain arbitrarily detained in appalling conditions. Belarus’ regime should release all political prisoners, immediately and unconditionally.”
Journalists, musicians among those arrested
The Belarusian human rights watchdog Viasna, which the government banned after declaring the group an extremist organisation, said many of those released on Wednesday had been sentenced to several years in prison.
The organisation named journalist Andrei Alyaksandrau, who had been serving a 14-year term, among those released. Alyaksandrau had been arrested in 2021 for allegedly “financing protest activities” alongside his girlfriend Iryna Zlobina, who was handed a nine-year sentence.
Alyaksandrau told Viasna he had lost 30kgs (66 pounds) while in captivity “for the motherland” but was “in a good mood”. He added that he was “very glad that these almost six years are over” and that he hadn’t seen Zlobina – whom he married in a pre-trial detention centre in 2022 – in four years.
Alongside Alyaksandrau, three other journalists – Dzmitry Navazhylau, Kiryl Pazniak and Liudmila Chekina – were released and immediately deported to Lithuania. Reporters Without Borders said it was “delighted” by their release but denounced their expulsion.
Exiled political opposition leader Svetlana Tsikhanouskaya said she was happy for the relatives of the 25 freed prisoners “who have been waiting for this day”. Her husband, Siarhei Tsikhanouski, was freed last year after spending five years in jail.
“Every release requires tremendous effort, and it is clear that [Lukashenko] does not want to release all political prisoners,” she wrote on X, noting that hundreds more remain behind bars.

title: Harris County to spend $3M on community safety programs leaders say have driven down crime
content:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.
HOUSTON — As executive director of the Harris County Domestic Violence Coordinating Council, Barbie Brashear has directly seen how domestic violence programs have helped families.
She also knows the dire consequences of such programs losing funding.
Brashear used her experiences — both personal and professional — to spearhead the Harris County Domestic Violence Coordinating Council program, which she hopes will become a model for cities across Texas and the nation. The program is unique in that it provides money to families affected by domestic violence to pay for a range of expenses like rent, utlity bills and groceries — with no questions asked.
“We’re leading the field and other people are looking at us to see what we’re doing,” Brasher said.
The domestic violence council works alongside the Holistic Assistance Response Team, or HART, and Relentless Interrupters Serving Everyone, known as RISE, two programs that are part of a community safety effort focused in cities and counties that surroundHouston.
HART sends behavioral health specialists to crisis situations, reducing jail time and connecting individuals to care. RISE is a public health initiative that aims to reduce gun violence through community-led interventions, like hospital bed visits for gunshot victims. The Domestic Violence Prevention and Intervention programs focus on directing federal grant funds to survivors and increasing community-based coordination between partners.
The three community safety programs were created in the wake of nationwide protests following the death of George Floyd. The Georgetown Law Center for Innovations in Community Safety recently released a report praising the progress these programs have made in making Harris County and surrounding areas safer with funding, resources, and intervention.
In areas where RISE operates, gun homicide rates have fallen faster than they have in Houston overall. The county’s Domestic Violence Prevention and Intervention programs have helped more than 5,000 survivors. And HART has freed thousands of hours for deputies and EMS to handle emergencies and connected more than 5,000 residents to care.
The programs were at risk of ending due to federal budget cuts growing economic uncertainty has led to a drop in philanthropic giving. Last week, Harris County commissioners gave initial approval to spend $3 million for them using local tax dollars. Final budget approval is expected Thursday. Commissioners are also expected to increase property taxes by 7.6% to help pay for these programs and close a $180 million budget deficit.
“Domestic violence resources have never been resourced properly from the beginning, ever. The demand has always been much higher than available resources,” Brasher said. “[COVID-19] funding got us a little closer, allowed us to invent and support and build some capacity, but it didn’t get all the way where we needed to be, and now those dollars are pulling back.”
Harris County — the state’s most populous with with more than 5 million people — plays a unique role in the Gulf Coast region. Programs started there often spread across county lines. The regional approach helps smaller rural counties that can’t often pay for their own safety net programs, Brashear said. She said without additional support from counties or state lawmakers, the future of many community safety programs in the rural parts of the state is grim.
“It’ll wipe those programs out,” she said. “Especially thinking about the surrounding counties around Harris County because what happens in the domestic violence field is when those families aren’t able to be served in that county, they’re coming into our county to be served because there is nothing for them.”
Abbie Kamin, Harris County’s attorney said the programs are working.
“The issues of domestic violence, gun violence, and mental health are pervasive and impact every corner of Harris County,” said Abbie Kamin, Harris County Attorney. “This is exactly the kind of innovative and data-driven work that we strive for when building the infrastructure that connects people with the resources they need most.”
While these community programs have seen success, funding streams for community safety programs are getting cut from multiple directions at once.
Last year, the Department of Justice terminated 365 previously awarded grants, with about $500 million in promised funds evaporating and affecting more than 550 organizations across 48 states. The Office on Violence Against Women has delayed or withheld money due to new federal cuts and restrictions on grant funding. The DOJ canceled 59 grants under the Victims of Crime Act. The Centers for Disease Control’s Division of Violence Prevention has seen layoffs, making it harder for community programs to connect with the federal government, and COVID-19 funds are simply running out.
“I can’t express enough how dire the situation is right now and how critical it is that we don’t move backward,” Brashear said.
Harris County safety net programs face major cuts
In April 2025, the federal government terminated 365 previously awarded grants, with about $500 million in promised funds evaporating and affecting more than 550 organizations across 48 states.
The White House has proposed another $850 million reduction in Justice Department grantmaking.
The Trump administration’s stated rationale for the cuts and new rules was that the programs were “funding DEI and cultural Marxism” rather than helping keep Americans safe, but a Council on Criminal Justice review found that about 60% of terminated grants made no reference to diversity, equity, race, gender, or related terms in their project descriptions. The council is a nonpartisan group that focuses on criminal justice and public safety.
“Prevention dollars have gone away completely, so prevention efforts aren’t being supported; DEI is definitely not being supported, and there has been an entire shift in priorities,” Brashear said.
The federal cuts are wreaking havoc on community safety programs in Texas.
Brashear said their domestic violence organizations in Harris County and Fort Bend County have lost collectively around $4 million. She said the cuts are leading to fewer staff to run shelters and longer wait times for survivors trying to access services in a county that has the highest domestic violence rate in the state.
“That is years of wisdom and years of experience walking out the door, and the turnover makes it even more expensive for agencies to function,” she said.
The Houston Area Women’s Center Domestic Abuse Response Team, which is on track to help up to 5,000 people this year, is facing operational reductions tied to the federal reconciliation bill, the Houston Chronicle reported earlier this year. Despite additional support from the county, HAWC has said it has been forced to lean more heavily on private fundraising because public funding is in flux.
And the Fort Bend Women’s Center, attributed layoffs at his facility to widespread grant cancellations and cuts from the Trump administration.
Trying to get county support
Harris County residents and advocates at public meetings have pleaded with the commissioners to fund the programs using local tax dollars.
“These are not charitable extras; they are the basic infrastructure people need to live safely and with dignity,” said Swathena Ryan, a worker for a Harris County domestic violence organization, told commissioners on Tuesday.
Commissioner Rodney Ellis, who represents many of the county’s Black and Hispanic neighborhoods, proposed last month investing an additional $3 million in HART, RISE, and the Domestic Violence Prevention and Intervention programs, aiming to make these programs permanent as demand for their services grows with the population. He said the proposed funds will raise the total annual investment in these community safety programs to around $14 million, or nearly 1% of the county’s law enforcement spending.
Of the $3 million, about $1.5 million will expand HART into a 24-hour, seven-days-a-week operation with staff; $600,000 will expand RISE into one additional neighborhood and fully staff its Cloverleaf neighborhood team; and $1 million will sustain domestic violence prevention.
Advocates say the three programs have done enough to earn a permanent place in the budget. HART has freed thousands of hours for deputies and EMS to handle emergencies and connected more than 5,000 residents to care. The neighborhoods where RISE is located experienced a 36% drop in crime — including a 48% drop in family violence and a 34% drop in aggravated robberies — in the first two years after the program was piloted there. The county’s Domestic Violence Prevention and Intervention programs have helped more than 5,000 survivors and their children with resources to safely leave abusive situations and delivered more than 20,000 hours of therapeutic care to 1,000 families.
Ellis said that for Harris County to meet the demands of its growing population, it can’t just prosecute people; it must also try to help them, and that requires funding the systems that support them.
“We hope to make Harris County a perfect model for other people to look at when you talk about community safety, not just in the state but even nationally,” he said.

title: Diabetes Education Program Tied to 57% Lower Early Death Risk in Major Slovak Cohort
content:
People with type 2 diabetes who completed a structured education program run by a Slovak health insurer were dramatically less likely to die over the following years than comparable patients who never took the classes, according to a large retrospective cohort study published in Diabetes Therapy. The analysis, drawing on administrative healthcare records from 2013 to 2024, found that participants in the education arm of a disease management program operated by Dôvera Health Insurance Company had a 57 percent lower risk of death from any cause during the first two years after starting the program, and a 32 percent lower risk in the years that followed. The findings arrive at a moment when health systems worldwide are searching for scalable, low-cost interventions that can complement the wave of powerful new diabetes drugs, and they suggest that one of the oldest tools in diabetes care—teaching patients how to manage their own disease—may be among the most powerful.
The study was possible because Slovakia offers an unusual natural experiment. Since the end of 2015, Dôvera, one of the country’s three mandatory health insurance companies and the insurer of roughly 1.77 million people, has run a disease management program for adults with type 2 diabetes. Enrollment in the program was required to access its benefits, but participation in the educational activities themselves was voluntary. That distinction turned out to be scientifically crucial. The program’s education, delivered by trained nurses using the Diabetes Conversation Maps tool alongside self-prepared materials, originally consisted of six to eight structured sessions spaced two to three weeks apart, each lasting about two hours and covering everything from dietary behavior and physical activity to complication prevention, medication adherence, and goal setting. From 2018 onward, the model was condensed to three or four sessions, with refresher contacts at one and two years, making education a continuous, long-term process rather than a one-off lecture series.
To isolate the effect of education, the researchers constructed three comparison groups from the insurer’s administrative database: patients who underwent education within the program, patients treated by diabetologists who participated in the program but whose patients never enrolled in it, and patients whose doctors were entirely outside the program. Using propensity score matching—a statistical technique that pairs participants with non-participants who share similar baseline characteristics—the team formed 4,702 matched triplets comprising 14,106 patients. All patients in the education group were successfully matched to controls from both reference groups. After matching, standardized mean differences for all measured covariates fell below 0.1, indicating that the groups were well balanced on the characteristics the data could capture. The matched cohort was 54.6 percent female, with a mean age of just over 60 years, and patients were followed for a median of 5.04 years, during which 1,695 deaths occurred.
The statistical analysis had to confront a complication that often arises in long-term observational studies: the effect of the intervention was not constant over time. Standard Cox regression assumes that the ratio of hazards between groups remains proportional across the follow-up period, but Schoenfeld residual tests rejected that assumption here. The researchers therefore turned to a piecewise Cox model, splitting follow-up into two pre-specified intervals: the first two years and everything after. The two-year cut-point was not arbitrary. In routine program practice, educators typically contact patients up to about two years after the initial course to review their status and offer re-education, marking a natural point at which the effect of the initial training might begin to fade—or be reinforced. Splitting the timeline also allowed the team to estimate effects in a period less contaminated by short-term selection dynamics, since neither patients nor physicians can reliably predict health trajectories far into the future when deciding whether to enroll in education.
The results were striking. Compared with patients receiving usual care outside the program, those who completed education had a 57 percent lower mortality risk in the first two years of follow-up, a hazard ratio of 0.43 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.30 to 0.60. Beyond two years, the protective effect attenuated but remained substantial and statistically significant, at 32 percent lower risk. Crucially, the second comparison group told a very different story. Patients treated by program-participating diabetologists who never took the education showed no survival benefit at all relative to the general reference population; in the weighted analysis their mortality risk was actually slightly higher. This is perhaps the study’s most provocative finding: the system-level machinery of a disease management program—financial incentives for physicians, feedback reports, specialist booking systems, shared data platforms—apparently did nothing for survival on its own. What mattered was the patient-facing component.
To guard against the possibility that the result was an artifact of the matching strategy, the researchers ran a parallel analysis using inverse probability of treatment weighting, a technique that reweights the entire sample to estimate what would happen if the whole insured population were offered education. The pattern held. Under this population-wide scenario, education was associated with a 60 percent lower mortality risk in the first two years and a 31 percent lower risk thereafter, both highly significant. Subgroup analyses found no meaningful interactions with sex or age across four age bands, suggesting the benefit was broadly distributed rather than concentrated in any particular demographic. The concordance across two independent statistical approaches strengthens confidence that the association is not simply a product of model specification.
The Slovak results fit into a growing international evidence base. Austria’s Therapie Aktiv program reported a 43 percent reduction in four-year mortality and a sustained 30 percent reduction over eight years in its early cohorts. Hong Kong’s RAMP-DM program documented a 55 percent reduction in all-cause mortality over a median follow-up of 9.5 years, alongside reductions in both macrovascular and microvascular complications. Randomized evidence points in the same direction: a meta-analysis of 42 trials including 13,017 patients found a 26 percent mortality reduction from self-management education, and a 2026 scoping review reported a 45 percent reduction when restricted to studies in which mortality was the primary outcome. The new study extends this evidence to a Central European population, adding geographic and demographic diversity to a literature the review’s authors noted is dominated by high-income countries.
Why would classroom sessions with nurses translate into fewer deaths? The authors argue the mechanisms are likely multifactorial. Prior research consistently shows that disease management programs improve glycemic control, lipid profiles, and blood pressure, and increase adherence to guideline-recommended screening and drug therapy. A 2012 meta-analysis of more than 140 quality improvement studies documented more frequent foot examinations, retinopathy screening, and kidney function monitoring, along with lower HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, and blood pressure. The researchers’ own earlier work on the same Slovak program showed increased frequency of HbA1c monitoring, suggesting improved process quality of care. Education may also reduce diabetes-related distress, which the team’s previous studies observed, potentially improving adherence to and understanding of needed lifestyle changes. The study period also overlapped with the introduction of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists, drugs with proven cardiovascular and renal benefits, and the program’s incentives may have eased administrative barriers to prescribing them—though the authors note that causes of death were unavailable, so any effect on COVID-19 era mortality cannot be confirmed.
The time-dependent pattern of the benefit offers its own lessons. A recent dose-response meta-analysis found that HbA1c improves rapidly—by about 1.3 percent within the first 30 weeks of face-to-face education—before gradually declining, mirroring the mortality trajectory seen here. Motivation is highest immediately after the course; behavioral effects fade without reinforcement; and after two years the program relies on patients initiating contact themselves. The authors also candidly acknowledge the specter of residual confounding. Participation was voluntary, and healthier or more motivated patients may be more likely to attend. Frail patients or those with subtle health deterioration may be quietly steered away from education by physicians even when they do not meet formal exclusion criteria—a hidden selection effect the researchers argue is most potent in the first two years and likely negligible beyond them, which is partly why the persistence of a significant benefit after the two-year mark is so reassuring.
The study’s limitations are real but bounded. Laboratory values were absent from the insurance data, precluding direct measurement of metabolic change; unmeasured factors such as frailty, functional status, and health literacy could still shape who enrolls and who survives; and only a randomized trial could fully eliminate confounding. Yet the strengths are considerable: a dataset covering a third of Slovakia’s population, follow-up stretching to eight years, rigorous matching with a strict intention-to-treat approach, and consistent results across complementary analytical methods. The practical implication is hard to escape. As new glucose-lowering drugs command headlines and budgets, the cheapest intervention in the diabetes toolkit—structured, sustained, nurse-led patient education—may deliver survival benefits that no amount of physician-side incentives or system engineering can match. Health systems designing the next generation of chronic disease programs, the authors suggest, should place education at the center rather than the periphery.

title: Keeping Haebangchon's spirit alive, one block party at a time
content:
As Haebangchon evolves, Block Party offers a glimpse of the creative community still at its heart
Last weekend, Haebangchon's bars, clubs and performance spaces played host to more than 100 live acts, ranging from punk bands and DJs to drag performers, wrestlers, magicians and swing dancers.
More than 1,000 people bought tickets to the fifth Block Party, held Sept. 11-13, making it the annual event's biggest edition yet, according to founder and main organizer Jamie Finn.
The festival is growing. But so is the attention surrounding the neighborhood it calls home.
"It's no secret to say that Haebangchon is changing," Finn told The Korea Herald. "There's a lot of gentrification at the moment, and that can be good and bad. It can help in some ways, but in other ways it can cause the loss of a certain identity."
Haebangchon, at the foot of Namsan in central Seoul, has long been shaped by change. In recent years, new restaurants, cafes and bars have increasingly drawn visitors to the neighborhood, while the once-struggling Shinheung Market has undergone years of regeneration to emerge as a popular destination.
For Finn, the answer is not to keep Haebangchon frozen in the past. Instead, he sees Block Party as a way to make sure the creative communities already established in the neighborhood remain part of its evolving identity.
"I think when someone sees something like Block Party, which channel the idea of what Haebangchon was and what some people still want it to be, I think it does make people rally behind it and say, 'This is a great idea. Let's keep that spirit alive,'" he said.
Building a party, block by block
Block Party began almost by accident.
In 2022, Finn and his team were hosting concerts to mark new issues of their independent culture magazine, then called Platform Magazine and now known as Debaser. When the shows began selling out, they started thinking bigger.
"We thought, why don't we do two concerts at the same time on the same street?" Finn recalled.
Two became three, then four. Eventually, the idea grew into the first Block Party: a one-day festival spread across five venues in Haebangchon and neighboring Gyeongnidan.
Five editions later, the festival is attracting attention from well beyond the neighborhood — including, this year, from BTS' RM.
Finn said RM came to the festival to see Sogumm, a member of alternative music collective Balming Tiger. He spotted RM outside the venue and approached him to thank him for coming.
"He told me I throw a great party," Finn recalled.
RM was "super nice," Finn said, and seemed genuinely curious about the festival, asking him questions about how it worked.
For Finn, the encounter reflected what Block Party is ultimately about: showing up for artists and supporting the community.
"At the end of the day, if you come to our festival and you show us support and you show us love, it means a lot to me, whoever you are," he said.
United by a shared love for HBC
For Finn, Block Party is not about creating something that exists for three days and disappears.
Many of the performers who fill its lineup are already part of Haebangchon's everyday creative life. Swing dancers meet every Sunday at Dialogue, one of the festival venues. Drag performances are held regularly in the neighborhood, while wrestlers return every month or two. Theater, live music and other performances continue throughout the year.
"A lot of those performers, they are here in the Haebangchon area every single week," Finn said, "We want us all to come together and show what Haebangchon can offer."
But Finn is also conscious that the spaces that sustain such communities cannot be taken for granted.
Small live music venues have also faced longstanding regulatory hurdles that have drawn renewed attention in recent months. In Busan, Ovantgarde was handed a two-month suspension after authorities said audience members were dancing during a performance, which is prohibited under the rules governing its general restaurant license.
Against that backdrop, Finn sees the support Block Party receives from Haebangchon's venues as particularly meaningful.
"Even if it's just for one weekend ... if we can keep that spirit of indie rock and the rebellious nature of punk and hip-hop, if we can bring that to Haebangchon for a few days and keep that going, I think that's great," he said.
"I think that's part of the reason why a lot of venues, they go that extra step and they go above and beyond to help us achieve that."
Beyond the block
For all its growth, Block Party itself remains a small operation. Finn organizes the festival with three others — Ethan Kim, Seok Jia and Kim Da-hyun, better known as Glass Girl — all while holding down full-time jobs. Much of the rest is made possible by participating venues and volunteers.
"We are quite good at creating the facade of being quite a professional festival," Finn said with a small laugh. "But the truth is we're just a bunch of friends trying to make a party for people to come to and have fun."
What has kept them doing it, he said, is the response from the people who come.
Some have told Finn they arrived in Korea knowing few people and little about its independent music scene, only to stumble across Block Party and find friends and communities they continued returning to.
"Since then they found a lot more friends, they found music scenes that they really like, and they found a way to feel more comfortable and more at home here," he said.
Stories like these offer a modest measure of the festival's success.
"Block Party is nothing without the people who come here and make it exciting."

title: BIT training surpasses annual target
content:
The Board of Industrial Training (BIT) has already surpassed its annual training target, reaching 3,310 Guyanese through 162 training projects across all 10 administrative regions as of September 9, 2026.
BIT Chief Executive Officer Richard Maughn on Friday, while delivering remarks at a graduation ceremony, said the achievement represents 138 per cent of the board’s annual target of 2,400 beneficiaries, underscoring the scale of government’s ongoing investment in technical and vocational skills development.
Of the 3,310 people reached this year, 1308 have graduated, 419 have completed training and are awaiting graduation, while 1,583 remain in training.
The programmes are designed to equip Guyanese with practical skills to improve their employment prospects and contribute to national development.
Maughn noted that the progress is part of a wider national skills-training drive implemented by BIT with government support.
“From 2020 to September 2026, the Board of Industrial Training has reached 19,600 beneficiaries through 1,061 courses,” Maughn said.
He emphasised that the investment in training is intended to translate into productive opportunities for beneficiaries beyond the classroom and certification process.
“The investment is intentional because it is the hope now that the investment has been made in you, that you will move out and not hang the certificate on a wall, but to do [and] practise that which you have acquired,” he exclaimed.
Maughn also urged the graduates to see these certifications as the beginning of their professional journey, encouraging them to continue developing their skills while demonstrating professionalism and responsible conduct in the workplace.
The expansion of BIT’s programmes is part of the government’s broader human-capital development agenda, with resources being directed towards giving Guyanese practical skills and opportunities to participate more meaningfully in the country’s growing economy. [DPI]

title: New county bus contracts to deliver drivers hefty pay rise
content:
New county bus contracts to deliver drivers hefty pay rise
New regional bus contracts will require drivers to be paid Estonia's average wage, increasing the amount of state funding needed to subsidize bus services.
Regional bus routes have for years operated under a sector-wide collective agreement between employers and employees that sets bus drivers' pay rates.
In 2025, the Association of Estonian Road Carriers and the Transport Workers' Union agreed that bus drivers would in future have to be paid Estonia's average wage. Contracts for regional bus routes are awarded for eight years and this year public transport centers will begin conducting the first procurements under the new terms.
"Over the next five years, all of our contracts will be renewed. Some have already been renewed, so to speak, while some are still being processed. Next year there will be two contracts and after that two contracts a year through 2031. The requirement to pay the average wage is now fully included in the new contracts," said Andrus Nilisk, executive director of the North Estonia Public Transport Center.
The calculation would be based on the previous year's average wage, or around €2,100, while bus drivers working under existing contracts that still have several years to run are being paid €1,500 this year. Their wages are increased through indexation.
"With the old contracts, wages also rise by €100 each year, so they will eventually reach roughly the same level, but under the new contracts the increase is steep," Nilisk said.
However, the wage increase would mean raising the state's annual taxpayer-funded subsidy.
"Labor costs account for about half of the price per route kilometer, so naturally this will have an impact on the subsidy. During the transition period, it will require around €1.5 million a year in additional subsidies. For the past five years, every year when the state budget has been adopted, there has not been enough funding to last through the end of the year and then additional money has been found midway through the year," said Kersten Kattai, director of the Association of Estonian Road Carriers.
The minimum salary for teachers is €1,970 this year. Estonia's median wage has been €1,750 this year. Minister of Regional Affairs Hendrik Johannes Terras would now have to seek additional funding for subsidies in order to pay bus drivers €2,100.
"I know that this agreement has been reached. It may have an impact on the bids submitted in terms of the price per kilometer. But given that relatively few of our contracts will be renewed next year, I don't expect it to have an impact on the budget," Terras said.

title: Blowhole nebulizer helps cure beluga whale’s pneumonia
content:
Pneumonia is a common affliction among whales and dolphins. In a first for marine mammals, veterinarians have used bacteria-killing viruses to treat a beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) with a drug-resistant infection.
Jetta, an 11-year-old beluga whale at Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut, developed chronic pneumonia caused by multi-drug-resistant E. coli bacteria. After powerful antibiotics proved mostly ineffective, the experts from the aquarium and University of Florida developed a bacteriophage treatment for Jetta, according to a statement sent to Popular Science. Bacteriophages are viruses that kill bacteria, and Jetta’s treatment used bacteriophages specifically chosen to fight the E. coli strain causing her infection.
“Whales, dolphins and seals, in the wild and under human care alike, are especially prone to gram-negative bacterial infections, a category of pathogens notoriously difficult to cure with antibiotics,” Molly Martony, senior veterinarian at Mystic Aquarium, tells Popular Science. “That’s the opposite of most land mammals, which more commonly battle gram-positive infections with a wider range of treatment options. As a result, marine mammals face multidrug-resistant infections far more often.”
The team delivered the treatment in various ways, including through a nebulizer. Jetta was trained to swim to the pool’s edge three times a day and inhale deeply through the nebulizer, which was crafted specially for a beluga blowhole. Jetta was treated over a year ago. Since then, her care team hasn’t found any evidence of recurrence, nor any negative side effects from the bacteriophage therapy.
“Bacteriophage therapy isn’t entirely new. It has also been used experimentally in humans. However, Jetta’s case highlighted something unexpected: the delivery method itself.” Martony explains. “Administering the phages via nebulization, essentially having her breathe them in, proved remarkably effective and stress-free. Human researchers have also started to show that it’s a route worth exploring in human medicine, potentially offering a faster, less invasive way to fight multidrug-resistant infections in people.”
Martony will be presenting the success at the University of Florida’s Phage Across One Health Symposium next month. She and partners at the University of Florida are also preparing the research for publication.

title: What makes a town a happy place to call home?
content:
In Mersing, happiness might look more like an evening by the sea, neighbours who know one another, a fishing trip with relatives or simply getting from one end of town to the other without sitting in traffic.
The coastal district was recently named one of Malaysia’s 10 happiest towns for 2026, alongside fellow Johor towns Kluang and Simpang Renggam. All three offer rather different versions of what a comfortable life can look like.
For Mersing resident Deiah Idris, 67, much of it comes down to family and familiarity. “I am happy because my family lives nearby, and many of my neighbours are also relatives,” she told Bernama.
“We often rent boats and go island-hopping together. It is really enjoyable.”
That easy connection between community and surroundings runs through much of life in Mersing, where fishing boats, the jetty and visitors heading to nearby islands are part of the everyday landscape.
The district is a gateway to islands including Pulau Aur, Pulau Tinggi, Pulau Besar, Pulau Pemanggil and Pulau Sibu, as well as Pulau Tioman in neighbouring Pahang.
Its location also gives Mersing an east-coast flavour reflected in local speech and food such as nasi dagang, keropok lekor and satar. Evenings can be spent playing dam soksek, a traditional board game similar to dam haji, or simply enjoying the coastline with family and friends.
Keeping the slower pace
District council president Abdul Karim Bakar believes Mersing does not need to chase every form of development to remain appealing.
“For some people, happiness means having shopping malls and entertainment, but we want to keep Mersing as it is so that people have the option of coming here to enjoy a peaceful atmosphere surrounded by nature,” he said.
Tourism is important, but locals are conscious of keeping it in proportion. Mersing Tourism Association secretary Ahmad Firdaus Shaik Omar said the district favours gradual growth rather than mass tourism that could put pressure on its beaches, islands and marine environment.
The attraction is easy to understand. Visitors come for island-hopping, snorkelling, diving and beaches, while the district’s marine and national parks add to its appeal for nature lovers.
Tourists do not necessarily see Mersing through rose-tinted glasses, either. Dutch visitor Jantine De Jong, 35, enjoyed the food and scenery on her second visit but felt the area around the jetty could offer more to do at night.
That tension may be part of Mersing’s challenge: adding enough to make life and travel more convenient without erasing the quietness people value in the first place.
Long-time residents Mohd Yassin Lazim, 72, and Zainab Abu Bakar, 73, seem happy with the balance they have found after more than two decades in their village.
“We feel comfortable because the village is peaceful and harmonious, and everyone is a good neighbour,” Yassin said.
Kluang and Simpang Renggam offer another version of the same idea. There, residents’ quality of life is supported more visibly by public amenities, recreational spaces, employment opportunities and the ability to get around without the pressures associated with much larger cities.
Kluang district officer Azurawati Wahid said a less congested lifestyle and better balance between work and personal time can contribute to both mental and physical wellbeing.
The two towns also have parks and public spaces where people can exercise, meet friends or spend time with family, while free local bus services and other amenities make everyday routines easier.
Kluang, in particular, offers vocational and skills-training opportunities as well as jobs in agriculture, manufacturing and services, giving some younger residents the option of building careers without immediately having to leave their home district.
Cost of living matters, too: being able to afford daily necessities, find work and still have time for family can influence wellbeing just as much as having access to entertainment or major commercial developments.
None of this, of course, means the three towns are perfect. Roads still need maintaining, public facilities need looking after, and residents still want efficient services, clean surroundings and safe neighbourhoods.
Perhaps that is the more useful way to think about a “happy town”. It is not somewhere without problems, but somewhere everyday life feels manageable – where people have enough of what they need, somewhere to breathe, and other people around whom they are glad to call neighbours.

A man with an uncommon type of motor neuron disease experienced improved symptoms and continued to work as a physician a year after becoming the first person to receive a drug designed to target the specific genetic mutation that causes his disease1. Researchers say the early results are exciting and lay the foundation for more treatments for neurodegenerative diseases caused by rare mutations.
The man had a slowly progressing form of motor neuron disease, also called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), caused by a rare mutation that leads to protein build-up that contributes to the death of motor neurons. He received an RNA treatment called antisense oligonucleotide therapy. Unlike typical gene therapy, which alters a person’s genes to treat a genetic disease, antisense oligonucleotide therapy, uses short strands of genetic material to target RNA produced by the gene and reduce how much protein is made. The results are published in Med this week.
Steve Vucic, a neurologist and ALS researcher at the University of Sydney in Australia, says the results are an “exciting first step”, although it is too early to know whether the treatment could stop disease progression or be a cure. That will require monitoring the trial participant for another two or three years and testing the drug in more people.
Similar antisense oligonucleotide therapies are the future of treatment for many people with ALS, says Fleur Garton, a neurological disease researcher at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia. Roughly 5–10% of people with ALS have a known genetic mutation. Antisense therapies seem to be safe and can be developed for people with common genetic mutations, for those with rare or even unique mutations, and for people whose disease is caused by multiple mutations, she adds.
Early encouragement
ALS causes motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord to die, leading to symptoms such as muscle weakness, difficulty speaking and progressive paralysis. Most people with the condition eventually require a ventilator to breathe, and death is often caused by respiratory failure. There is no cure and treatment options are limited; The average life expectancy after diagnosis is about two to five years.
The trial participant’s disease is caused by a mutation in the gene CHCHD10, found in fewer than 1% of people who inherit ALS. This gene encodes a protein that enables mitochondria — the organelles that generate the energy needed to power cells — to function properly. Defects in the gene can damage the mitochondria and are thought to contribute to the death of neurons.
The patient received three 50-milligram doses of the drug in his spine, followed by three 75-milligram doses, between April 2024 and April 2025. He did not experience any serious negative side effects, the authors reported. He also showed no signs of cognitive decline, a common symptom of ALS.
A year after the first dose, his blood levels of neurofilament light chain proteins — which are produced by damaged neurons, and so are used as a biomarker for ALS progression — had reduced to the normal reference range. Vucic says this suggests that the treatment could be preserving the neurons in the man’s brain.
Scores on a test that measures motor skills, breathing and neurological function had improved, and other scores for breathing and cognition remained stable. Some people with ALS experience short-term improvements in symptoms without treatment, although study co-author Björn Oskarrson, a neurologist at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, says that sustained improvement without treatment is rare.
Antisense therapies have been developed to target more common gene mutations that cause ALS, but those therapies took at least a decade to make. By contrast, the drug that targets CHCHD10 took only three years to develop, says Oskarrson. Being able to develop a drug to target a specific person’s mutation, test it in animals and then give it to the person within their lifespan was amazing, he adds.

title: Immigration Lawyer John Dutton Frees Cuban from 'Death Row' Detention Center
content:
Walter Carmenate Paradela, a Cuban holding permanent residency in the United States, has walked free from the Bluebonnet detention center—referred to by inmates as "death row"—without paying a single dollar in bail, all thanks to the dedicated efforts of the Houston-based John Dutton Law Firm.
Describing his release with disbelief, Walter Carmenate shared, "I'm the second person to leave that center. Someone else got out first, but they had to pay $40,000 in bail. I walked out without any bail; I'm just free. No one could believe it, not even the officers there thought I would leave without paying a cent."
The Unexpected Turn of Events
The trouble began with a minor traffic violation related to a car license from Florida that Walter had not yet updated in Houston. The situation worsened when he provided the court with all the vehicle's documentation, which belonged to a friend who had given him fake insurance. An earlier attorney, who represented him in that matter, advised him to plead guilty, falsely assuring him there would be no immigration repercussions—a grave mistake in hindsight.
Walter Carmenate was eventually arrested on July 27, 2026, during a meeting with his new parole officer in Amarillo, Texas. He was transported, shackled at the feet, hands, and waist, in a van for nearly four hours to the Bluebonnet facility in Anson, Texas, where he spent 51 grueling days. "Those 51 days were the hardest for me," he recounted. "I felt as if I had been there for over a year."
"You know what they call that place: death row. Nobody escapes from there. Everyone gets deported," he said.
Legal Maneuvers That Led to Freedom
Attorney John Dutton detailed the strategy that led to his client's release and the retention of his green card. According to Dutton, securing a habeas corpus in Bluebonnet is particularly challenging due to its location in the Northern District of Texas, a federal jurisdiction with few precedents favorable to immigrants.
The legal breakthrough came by pinpointing the actual date of Walter's entry into the U.S., placing him outside the five-year period the Department of Homeland Security cited for deportation. This technicality could not be disputed by the government, prompting the judge to close the case without imposing bail.
When asked about his gratitude, Walter Carmenate was quick to express his deepest appreciation: "I'm thankful to the lawyers, but especially to my wife, who was always there, never leaving me alone."
Support and Testimonies
An office client named Alexandra also shared her experience during the interview: "I am a witness to their results and especially to the heart with which this wonderful team works. I experienced firsthand their dedication, commitment, and support during one of the toughest times in my life." Dutton humbly replied, "We strive to do our job as best as we can."
Walter Carmenate's ordeal highlights a recurring pattern among Cuban permanent residents detained by ICE: minor criminal records, sometimes stemming from poor legal advice, triggering retroactive deportation proceedings in an increasingly restrictive immigration climate.
As the interview concluded, Dutton issued a caution for those with asylum cases on appeal before the BIA: they must timely pay the annual $102 fee to prevent their cases from being dismissed. The lawyer also advises eligible permanent residents to pursue citizenship promptly as a primary legal shield against such processes.
Walter Carmenate's case is just one among many illustrating the complex immigration landscape in the United States. Stay informed on detentions, bails, and immigrant rights in our U.S. Immigration section.
